increments.title: Frontend shows no phase banner; Design release 1 carries an Alpha banner with a feedback link on every page
increments.detail:
No page in the service carries a phase banner. The shared layout builds the GOV.UK header, the service navigation, the signed-in bar and the breadcrumbs, and goes straight into the page content with nothing between (src/server/app/shared/layout.njk:19-53). There is no govukPhaseBanner import and no phase-banner markup anywhere in src/server, and none of the 67 captured frontend screens renders one. So a user is never told the service is in Alpha and is never offered a way to give feedback.

Every one of the 60 captured Design release 1 screens opens with a phase banner directly under the service navigation: a grey "Alpha" tag followed by "This is a new service. Help us improve it and give your feedback by email.", with "give your feedback by email" as a link (app/views/dashboard.html:15-20). Each view declares it in its own beforeContent block rather than in the layout, so the banner is repeated per view but is present on all of them — and because the Prototype Kit's own branded layout carries no phase banner, the banner and its wording are something the designers wrote on every page by hand rather than furniture they inherited, which makes it a deliberate decision of the design.

Render a govukPhaseBanner in the shared layout's beforeContent block, above the breadcrumbs and back link, so it appears on every page including the dashboard: tag text "Alpha", body "This is a new service. Help us improve it and give your feedback by email." with the last five words as a link. The banner text belongs in src/server/app/shared/copy.en.js beside the existing layout copy at :10-21, with a Welsh pair in copy.cy.js. Design release 1 points the feedback link at a placeholder, so this service needs a real destination — a feedback form or a mailto address — decided before the work lands; the banner itself does not depend on it.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding phase-banner markup in the captured DOM of any frontend screen, or a Design release 1 root view whose beforeContent block omits the banner.

openQuestions: Where should the phase banner's feedback link point? The increment's own difference states Design release 1 uses a placeholder href and that this service 'needs a real destination — a feedback form or a mailto address — decided before the work lands'. That decision was made by the implementing agent, not the service team: backlog notes record the RULING href="mailto:APHAServiceDesk@apha.gov.uk", ending 'Flagged to a human for confirmation', and gate was null so nothing held the increment. The address is currently shipped as landed in src/server/app/shared/layout.njk:15, the feedbackUrl set above the blocks; the anchor that consumes it sits in the beforeContent block at layout.njk:47. The concern is that this codebase presents that mailbox as the TECHNICAL SUPPORT desk, not a feedback channel: src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/confirmation/template.njk:32-36 renders copy.help.technicalHelp = 'Contact the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) if you need technical help with this service:' (confirmation/copy/copy.en.js:28-29) with 'Telephone: 0330 041 6999' and 'Monday to Friday, 8:30am to 5pm'. The phase banner asks a different question — alpha usability feedback — and the shared layout renders on roughly 30 pages, so an unconfirmed destination ships service-wide. ACTION FOR THE SERVICE TEAM: confirm APHAServiceDesk@apha.gov.uk as the alpha-feedback destination and record that decision here, or supply the agreed feedback form URL / team mailbox and change the feedbackUrl set at layout.njk:15 together with the two places that pin the href — the feedbackAnchor constant in the 'alpha phase banner' describe of src/server/app/shared/layout.test.js, and the FEEDBACK_MAILTO constant at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/dashboard.fit.spec.js:14. Deferred rather than fixed in this increment because code cannot settle it — no alternative destination exists in the repo to substitute, and inventing a /feedback route would expand the increment's blast radius.

provenance.note: No phase banner anywhere in the frontend; DR1 carries an Alpha banner with a feedback link on all its screens. Same ask, same placement in beforeContent, same copy home, and both independently flag that the feedback link's real destination has to be decided because DR1's href is a placeholder. A adds one useful argument C does not: the banner is authored per-view in DR1 rather than injected by the Prototype Kit, so it is a deliberate design decision and not kit furniture.

openQuestions: Where should the section caption sit on the five pages whose h1 is produced inside the form — cph-number (label as heading), import-reason, import-purpose, transporters and transporters-select (legend as heading)? This increment emits the caption immediately before <form> on all five (e.g. src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/import-purpose/template.njk:9 with the h1 inside the govukRadios legend at template.njk:17-21), so the caption is outside the fieldset and outside the form group. Two consequences, both verified: (1) on an error render govuk-frontend applies .govuk-form-group--error{padding-left:15px;border-left:5px solid} (node_modules/govuk-frontend/dist/govuk/govuk-frontend.min.css) to the group containing the fieldset, so the h1 shifts 20px right and sits inside the red bar while the caption stays flush at the content edge — caption and heading visibly misalign; (2) because the caption is outside the fieldset, a screen reader announcing the legend as focus enters the radio group reads the question with no section name, so the context this increment adds is available to sighted users only. GOV.UK's own guidance is the opposite of what we shipped — dist/govuk/core/_typography.mixin.scss:62 reads '// Captions to be used inside headings' — and the fix would be to build the legend/label html (`{% set legendHtml %}{{ sectionCaption(caption) }}{{ copy.legend }}{% endset %}`) and pass it as `legend: { html: legendHtml, isPageHeading: true }`. DEFERRED rather than fixed in this increment because it is not a like-for-like markup swap: putting the caption inside the h1 changes the heading's accessible name from e.g. 'Reason for import' to 'About the consignment Reason for import', which breaks the getByRole('heading', { name: copy.legend }) locators used across the existing fit specs (import-reason.fit.spec.js:29,37, import-purpose, transporters, transporters-select, cph-number) and changes the rendered DOM order the increment's FALSIFIED BY clause is measured against. ACTION: decide with design/accessibility whether the caption goes inside the legend/label heading on these five pages (GDS-correct, needs the fit-spec locators reworked and the parity corpus re-captured) or stays as a sibling before the form (current shape, needs the error-state misalignment accepted or a spacing rule added). Whichever is chosen, the placement assertion added to section-caption.fit.spec.js for the legend-heading page must be updated to match.
increments.title: DR1 names the section of the notification above each page heading; the frontend gives 28 of its 33 pages no caption at all.
increments.detail:
Almost every page opens straight into its h1 with nothing above it, so a user part-way through a long notification cannot tell from the page which part of the notification they are in. On the CPH page the heading "County Parish Holding (CPH)" is the first thing under the status strip — src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/cph-number/template.njk:11-23 renders the label as the page heading with nothing before it. Only five of the 33 captured screens carry a caption at all: the five address pickers, which say "Consignment addresses" from their own template at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/party-picker.njk:7 rather than from anything shared. The remaining 28 have none.

A short grey caption sits above the h1 naming the section of the notification the page belongs to. The same CPH page reads "Consignment parties" above "Add the county parish holding number (CPH)" — app/views/cph-number.html:31-34 is one of 35 of the 40 captured DR1 screens that carry one. The captions in use are: "About the consignment" (origin, reason for import, what are you importing, consignment details, identification details), "Commodity details" (additional details), "Consignment parties" (roles and addresses, the address picker, CPH, permanent address), "Movement" (transit countries), "Transport and arrival" (transporter, arrival details), "Documents" (upload documents), "Add a new transporter" (the three transporter-add pages) and "Dashboard" (the dashboard). The five DR1 screens without one are the overview, the review page, the contact address page, the declaration and the confirmation.

Add a caption slot to the shared page-heading pattern so each journey page can name its section, then set it on the 21 of those 28 pages whose DR1 counterpart has one, using DR1's section names above. Seven of the 28 do not get a caption: DR1 deliberately gives none to its overview, review, contact-address, declaration or confirmation pages, so the frontend's overview, check-your-answers, contact, declaration and confirmation stay bare; and delete-notification and cancel-amend have no DR1 counterpart at all. The caption belongs in the view model rather than in the template copy of each feature, because the value is a property of where the page sits in the journey — the hub already knows its section grouping and builds it at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/flow/task-rows.js:27-59, so derive the caption from there rather than hard-coding a string per page. That makes the work a layout change plus one string per section rather than a decision taken 21 times. This changes no question and no answer; it is a heading-pattern change only. The five existing captions are handled separately: they are present but name the wrong section.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding a caption rendered above the h1 on a frontend journey page other than the five address pickers — any element carrying caption text between the status strip and the h1 in the 33 captured DOMs.

increments.title: The only captioned pages in the frontend name the section "Consignment addresses"; DR1 calls the same section "Consignment parties".

The string is set once at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/copy/copy.en.js:42 and rendered at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/party-picker.njk:7, with a Welsh pair at copy.cy.js:43. increments.title: Frontend's service navigation carries no items; Design release 1 offers Dashboard, Address book, Manage account and Log out on every page
increments.detail:
The service navigation bar holds the service name and nothing else — src/server/app/shared/layout.njk:27-32 calls govukServiceNavigation with serviceName and serviceUrl and passes no navigation array, so the bar renders as a single link reading "Import notification service". Below it a separate right-aligned strip shows the signed-in user's email address and a "Sign out" link (src/server/common/components/service-header/template.njk:9-29). "Manage account" and "Address book" appear nowhere in the service: neither string occurs in any of the 67 captured frontend screens. So from any page there is no way to reach the dashboard, the address book or an account page other than by using the browser or the service-name link.

Every Design release 1 page carries a four-item service navigation to the right of the service name: Dashboard, Address book, Manage account and Log out (app/views/layouts/main.html:104-127). The item matching the current page is marked active and rendered with aria-current, so on the dashboard "Dashboard" is underlined. There is no separate signed-in strip and the user's identity is not shown; sign-out lives in the navigation as "Log out". The bar is authored rather than inherited from the Prototype Kit — the layout builds the four items explicitly, and the design-release-2 branch above them carries a fifth, which is how you can tell the item list is a per-release decision rather than a default.

Pass a navigation array to govukServiceNavigation in src/server/app/shared/layout.njk:27-32 with the four items, and set the active item per page so the current section is marked. Move sign-out out of the bespoke strip at src/server/common/components/service-header/template.njk:9-29 and into the navigation as "Log out", which leaves that strip carrying the user's email alone — decide whether it stays at all, since Design release 1 shows no signed-in identity. The item labels belong in src/server/app/shared/copy.en.js under `layout`, with a Welsh pair in copy.cy.js. Two of the four already have somewhere to point: Dashboard is the existing notifications list at `/`, and Log out the existing `/auth/sign-out`. The other two need a destination this service does not yet have: "Address book" points at the address-book UI being built in trade-imports-ins-frontend, and "Manage account" has no owner named anywhere. Add the items with real hrefs where they exist and agreed placeholders where they do not — Design release 1 itself points both at a placeholder. Whether the address book belongs to this service is a separate question, recorded under address-book--saved-address-book-pages-absent.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding a navigation item — any of Dashboard, Address book, Manage account or Log out — in the govuk-service-navigation list of any captured frontend screen.

increments.title: DR1 lets a user narrow the notification list by date — Today, Tomorrow, Next seven days, or a start and end date chosen from a calendar; the frontend has no date filter.
increments.detail:
The dashboard has one filter, a keyword box searching the reference number (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:41-55). A user cannot ask which consignments are arriving today, or in the next week, or between two dates. Arrival date is shown on every card and can be sorted on, but it cannot be filtered on.

The filter sidebar's third collapsible section, "By date", holds three radios — Today, Tomorrow, Next seven days — followed by a "Select date range" block with the hint "For example, 27/3/2026" and two date fields, Start date and End date. Each date field carries a calendar button that opens a month calendar with previous/next month controls and Select and Close buttons (app/views/dashboard.html:165-226). Like the rest of the sidebar it is markup only — the sidebar is in no form, and getDashboardViewModel reads dateRange, startDate and endDate but never filters the list by any of them (app/routes.js:7143-7146).

Add a date filter to the dashboard's filter panel: the three relative-range radios and a start/end date pair using the MoJ date picker DR1 uses. Which date it filters on has to be stated, and the design does not state it anywhere — the section is headed "By date", its visually hidden legend reads "Choose a date range" and the two fields are only "Start date" and "End date". Two things point at the same answer without settling it: DR1's card labels the date "Arrival date at destination", which is the only date on a DR1 card, and the shortcuts Today, Tomorrow and Next seven days all point at a future date, which on a notification is the arrival date. So arrival at destination is the reading, but the prototype never demonstrates it and the design never says it. The list read accepts page, sort and reference number only (src/server/app/services/persistence/records/real/lifecycle/read.js:26-34), so the notifications endpoint has to accept a date range before the control can do anything. Build the relative radios on top of the same range parameter rather than as three more parameters.

increments.title: DR1 groups the dashboard filters into three collapsed sections a user opens one at a time — Search by, Status, By date; the frontend's filter panel is a single always-open block.
increments.detail:
The panel beside the list is headed "Filter notifications" as a third-level heading, with its one control — the keyword box and its Search button — always visible below it (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:38-56). With one control there is nothing to group, so the panel is as tall as its contents.

DR1's panel carries the plain label "Filter notifications" and then three collapsed sections, each a summary row with a chevron: Search by, Status and By date (app/views/dashboard.html:83-227). On first load all three are shut, so the panel is three rows tall and the page opens with the list, not the filters, in the reader's eye; opening a section reveals only that section's controls. dr1-dashboard is the shut state and dr1-dashboard-filters-open is all three open.

Group the dashboard filters into three collapsible sections under a "Filter notifications" label, shut on load, using the same three section names DR1 uses. This is the container the other three filter findings put controls into, so it wants doing first or alongside them — on its own it collapses one keyword box behind a chevron, which is worse than what is there now. Match DR1's heading treatment too: DR1 labels the panel rather than heading it, so the sections are the only headed things inside it. The two runs band this differently and it is worth saying why. Run C bundles the sections in with the commodity, consignee, status and date filters as one needs-backend finding, which parks the only part of the filter panel that could be built today behind a contract change. Run A raises it on its own and bands it frontend-work, which is the band kept here, because the collapsing behaviour is native details and summary markup: it needs no form, no script and no query parameter, and it is the only part of DR1's filter panel that genuinely does what it appears to do — every other control in that sidebar sits outside the page's only form and is wired to nothing. What turns on the answer is whether any of this filter work can start before the notifications endpoint grows.

increments.title: DR1 searches the notification list on three terms — keyword or notification number, commodity code or name, and consignee or importer; the frontend's one search box matches the reference number only.
increments.detail:
The filter panel holds one text box labelled "Keyword or reference" and a Search button. The label promises a keyword search but the value is passed straight through as a reference-number match — the controller reads request.query.referenceNumber and hands it to the list read under that name (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/controller.js:54-59), which puts it on the notifications request as referenceNumber (src/server/app/services/persistence/records/real/lifecycle/read.js:30-34). A user who types a commodity or a consignee's name gets no results, and a trader with a long list has no way to narrow it to one commodity or one consignee.

The sidebar's first collapsible section, "Search by", holds three separate labelled boxes: "Keyword or notification number", "Commodity code or name" and "Consignee/Importer" (app/views/dashboard.html:87-132). The three are markup only — they sit outside every form on the page, and getDashboardViewModel never reads a keyword, commodity or consignee value and never filters the list (app/routes.js:7138-7255). DR1 states which three things a user should be able to search on; it does not demonstrate any of them working.

Replace the single box with the three DR1 asks for, and make each one search what its label promises. The frontend already carries the reference-number search, so the keyword box is the existing one relabelled and widened from an exact reference match to a keyword match: "Keyword or reference" becomes "Keyword or notification number", the label the design uses. Commodity and consignee are new: the notifications endpoint accepts page, sort and reference number and nothing else (src/server/app/services/persistence/records/real/lifecycle/read.js:26-34), so both need a search parameter added to the contract, and consignee matching needs the search to reach the party names the address book holds rather than the notification record alone.

FALSIFIED BY: Typing a commodity name or a consignee name into the frontend's search box and getting the matching notification back.

increments.title: DR1 lets a user narrow the notification list to one status from a list of seven; the frontend offers no status filter at all.
increments.detail:
The whole of the filter surface is a single "Keyword or reference" box with a Search button (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:38-56). A user with a long list who wants to see only their drafts, or only the ones that have been submitted, has no way to ask for that.

The filter sidebar carries a collapsible "Status" section holding a single select labelled Status, offering Select one, Draft, Submitted, In progress, Approved, Action required, Rejected and Complete (app/views/dashboard.html:134-163). The control is markup only: the sidebar sits outside every form on the page — the rendered dashboard has exactly one form and it is the sort toolbar — and getDashboardViewModel reads query.status but never filters the list with it (app/routes.js:7147, 7166-7171). So DR1 states the requirement to filter by status and demonstrates the control, but a click in the prototype changes nothing.

Add a status filter to the dashboard's filter panel, offering the status values the real service actually has. Two things have to be settled before it can be built. First, the list read only accepts page, sort and reference number today (src/server/app/services/persistence/records/real/lifecycle/read.js:26-34), so filtering by status needs the notifications endpoint to accept a status parameter. Second, DR1's seven-value list is larger than the four statuses the frontend can produce — Draft, Submitted, Amending and Deleted, held as a tag map at src/server/app/shared/kit.js:34-51 and named in shared copy at src/server/app/shared/copy.en.js:47-51 — and the prototype's seven are a fixture rather than a statement about the service, so the option set has to be agreed against the statuses the service really holds rather than copied from the prototype's select.

The claim that the rendered dashboard has exactly one form and it is the sort toolbar is literally true — I counted the form elements in capture/html/prototype/dr1-dashboard.html and there is one — and the seven status values plus Select one are exactly the option elements in that captured DOM. The control is more inert than the finding says: because the root mount carries no design-release-2 session flag, statusFilterItems comes back null, and the root view hardcodes its option list with no selected flag, so DR1's status select does not even remember a chosen value across a page load. It is dead in both directions. Two smaller notes. The claim that the frontend can produce four statuses is one too many — deleted rows are stripped from the list at controller.js:61, so a dashboard card can only ever show Draft, Submitted or Amending — which makes the gap against DR1's seven wider, not narrower. increments.title: The dashboard shows no "At a glance" summary; Design release 1 opens it with counts of alerts, errors and messages waiting for the trader
increments.detail:
The dashboard goes straight from the start button to "Your notifications" and the list (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:27-56). There is nothing above the list summarising what needs the trader's attention, and no alerts, errors or messages anywhere in the service — the words appear in none of the 67 captured frontend screens. A trader with a notification the authorities have rejected learns it only by reading the status tag on that notification's card.

Between the start button and the notification list Design release 1 shows a section headed "At a glance" holding three cards side by side: Alerts, Errors and Messages (app/views/dashboard.html:39-77). Each card shows an icon, a count, and a link — "View alerts", "View errors", "View messages" — that takes the trader to the detail. The counts come from the view model's alertCounts, which hard-codes {alerts: 0, errors: 0, messages: 0} for every release (app/routes.js:7207-7211), so all three read 0 in the capture, and every link is an href="#" placeholder. The design states that the three lists exist and are reachable but not what they contain, and the prototype never demonstrates the band carrying anything.

Add a summary section to the dashboard above the notification list, headed "At a glance", with a card per category showing the count and a link through to it. Three things have to exist before it is more than decoration: a source of alert, error and message counts for the signed-in organisation, which no service in this workspace exposes today and which the notification contract does not carry — the list read asks the notifications endpoint for page, sort and reference number only (src/server/app/services/persistence/records/real/lifecycle/read.js:26-34) and the row model carries reference, status, commodity, origin, arrival, consignor, consignee and two dates (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/view-model/row/index.js:10-29), so nothing in the frontend's record store expresses an alert, an error or a message at all; a decision on what an alert, an error and a message are, since Design release 1 shows the categories and not their contents; and the three destination pages the links point at, which Design release 1 leaves as placeholders. The section itself can be built and shown with zero counts before any of that lands, so the visual work does not have to wait, but the section is not worth shipping until the counts are real.

increments.title: The frontend puts a breadcrumb trail above the back link on almost every page; DR1 has no breadcrumbs anywhere in the service.
increments.detail:
Every page inside a notification opens with a two-step breadcrumb trail — "Your notifications" linking to the dashboard, then the page's own title — sitting above the back link. 30 of the 33 captured screens show a trail with items in it. The trail is always exactly two steps regardless of how deep the page sits, so on the address picker it reads "Your notifications > Place of origin" and says nothing about the addresses hub the user came through. The two dashboard screens are worse: they render the breadcrumb navigation landmark with an empty list inside it, so a screen-reader user is announced a breadcrumb that contains nothing; the empty component paints no rule and no background, so what a sighted user loses to it is the vertical space above the h1 rather than a visible bar. Only the overview page renders no breadcrumb markup at all, and the confirmation page is the reverse case — it carries the trail with no back link beneath it, so there the trail is the only backward-looking chrome on the page. The layout builds the trail by default for any page with a title at src/server/app/shared/layout.njk:41-49, using the copy at src/server/app/shared/copy.en.js:14-16.

There are no breadcrumbs on any of DR1's 40 captured screens. A user's route back up is the service navigation bar at the top of the page — Dashboard, Address book — and the back link, and nothing else. DR1 states no third route out of a page.

Remove the breadcrumb trail, leaving the back link as the only in-page route backwards. There are five places to touch, not one: the default trail in the shared layout at src/server/app/shared/layout.njk:41-49; the trail builder at src/server/app/shared/paths.js:12-15, which hard-codes "Your notifications" rather than reading it from copy; the `breadcrumbs` leaf in src/server/app/shared/copy.en.js:14-16 and its Welsh pair; and the global Nunjucks default `breadcrumbs: []` at src/config/nunjucks/context/context.js:36, which is outside src/server/app and is what makes the two dashboard screens render an empty breadcrumb landmark; and the breadcrumbs branch of the shared kit helper at src/server/app/shared/kit.js:116, which assembles the component from that seed and goes dead with the rest. Only one page passes an explicit value — src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/check-answers/controller.js:72 — and the overview passes `breadcrumbs: false` at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/hub/controller.js:168; both callers go with the rest. This should not land before the service navigation carries a Dashboard item, because until it does the breadcrumb is the only always-present link to the notification list and removing it would leave a user mid-notification with nothing but the back link. Once the nav is populated the two say the same thing twice, in two places, which is what DR1 avoids.

increments.title: Each dashboard notification card lists eight facts over three rows; Design release 1's card shows four over two
increments.detail:
A notification card carries its reference as a heading and then eight labelled facts in three rows of three: Commodity, Origin, Arrival at destination; Consignee, Consignor, Status; Date created, Date submitted (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:113-154, values built at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/view-model/row/index.js:10-22). On a draft, five of the eight are blank — the picture of fe-dashboard-populated shows Commodity, Arrival at destination, Consignee, Consignor and Date submitted all empty — so the card is mostly labels with nothing beside them.

Design release 1's card carries the reference and four facts in two rows of two: Commodity and Status on the first row, Origin and "Arrival date at destination" on the second (app/views/dashboard.html:265-292). Consignee, consignor and the created and submitted dates are not shown. Status sits on the top row beside the commodity rather than buried in the middle of the card, so the tag is the second thing a trader reads. The austerity is a decision about the whole card rather than about the two party names alone: the prototype's fixture record also holds a submitted date, a commodity label, a category label and a quantity, and the root card prints none of those either.

Cut the card down to the four facts the design shows, in the design's order and layout: Commodity and Status on the first row, Origin and Arrival date at destination on the second. Drop the Consignee, Consignor, Date created and Date submitted pairs from src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:113-154 and the matching keys from the row view model at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/view-model/row/index.js:10-22 and from the copy at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/copy/copy.en.js:15-26. This is one decision about what a card is for: Design release 1's card identifies a consignment by what is coming, from where and when, and leaves the parties to the notification itself. The arrival label changes wording in the same copy block and is raised on its own as inc-016, which wants doing in the same pass. Which links the card offers is a separate question and is not changed here.

increments.title: The dashboard's results count changes shape as the list grows and capitalises Results; Design release 1 states one range in sentence case — "Show 1-4 of 4 results"
increments.detail:

Design release 1 always states a range: "Show 1-4 of 4 results", in sentence case, printed above the sort control (app/views/dashboard.html:236). It gives the range even when everything fits on one page, and results is lower case throughout. The prototype's count builder (app/routes.js:6700-6714) has that one shape and an empty-list line reading "Show 0 of 0 results".

Rewrite the count strings to the design's shape — "Show {start}-{end} of {total} results", lower-case, hyphenated range, stated even for a single page — in src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/copy/copy.en.js:37-47. The count builder at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/notification-helper.js already knows the start, end and total, so no new data is needed. increments.title: The dashboard's browser tab reads "Import notification service | Import notification service"; Design release 1 names the page "Dashboard"
increments.detail:
The layout builds every page title as the page name, a pipe, then the service name (src/server/app/shared/layout.njk:17). The dashboard's page name is the service name — copy.title is "Import notification service" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/copy/copy.en.js:2), passed as pageTitle at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/controller.js:70 — so all seven captured dashboard screens have a title reading "Import notification service | Import notification service". A trader with several tabs open cannot tell the dashboard from any other page of the service, and a screen reader announces the service name twice.

Design release 1 names the page "Dashboard" and shows the same word as the caption above the heading, while the heading itself stays "Import notification service" (app/views/dashboard.html:12). The tab reads "Dashboard - Import notification service - GOV.UK". The same word is also the active item in the service navigation bar, so Design release 1 names the page Dashboard in three places — the tab, the caption and the navigation — and the frontend names it in none. Every other Design release 1 page names itself after what it asks, and none repeats the service name.

Give the dashboard a page name of its own — "Dashboard" — and keep the h1 as the service name, which is what the design does. That means separating the title passed as pageTitle at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/controller.js:70 from the heading rendered at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:27, and adding a second key beside copy.title in src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/copy/copy.en.js:2. The separator and the absence of a "GOV.UK" suffix are not in question here; only the page name is — but the separate finding on title format rewrites the same string for every page, so the two want doing in one pass rather than rewriting the dashboard's title twice.

increments.title: Choosing a sort order on the dashboard does nothing until the trader also presses "Update sort"; Design release 1 shows the select with no button beside it
increments.detail:
A secondary button labelled "Update sort" sits immediately to the right of the sort select and submits the form that carries it (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:63-82). Changing the select alone re-orders nothing; the trader has to change it and then press the button. The same pattern applies to the filter panel, whose "Search" button is the only way to apply the keyword.

Design release 1's toolbar holds the results count and the sort select and nothing else (app/views/dashboard.html:231-251). There is no button beside the select and none anywhere in the filter panel, so on the face of the design a choice takes effect on its own.

This finding may be wrong, and the reason it is banded disputed is that Design release 1 gives no evidence its select works at all: it is inert in three separate ways. The prototype's dashboard route reads a sort query parameter but never applies it — getDashboardViewModel (app/routes.js:7138-7255) passes the value to the select so the right option shows as chosen and into the pagination links, and orders the notification list nowhere. The select sits in a GET form that carries no submit button. And nothing else on the page submits that form either: the prototype ships no dashboard script that submits on change, none of the twenty-one files in app/assets/javascripts mentioning the sort control. So Design release 1's sort control changes nothing whichever way it is driven, and the absent button could equally be a design decision to apply on change or an unimplemented corner of a prototype. Settle it before doing anything: if it is a design decision, the frontend should submit the form when the select changes and drop the "Update sort" button from src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/template.njk:63-82, with a no-JavaScript fallback that keeps the button visible. If it is prototype incompleteness, the frontend is already right and this finding is struck.

FALSIFIED BY: A Design release 1 dashboard capture in which changing the "Sort by" select re-orders the list without any further action by the user.

increments.title: The dashboard's sort control names a field and a direction in four options; Design release 1 names what the trader wants in three — newest first, oldest first, arrival date
increments.detail:
The list is headed by a "Sort by" select offering four orderings: "Arrival (newest to oldest)", "Arrival (oldest to newest)", "Date created (newest to oldest)" and "Date created (oldest to newest)" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/copy/copy.en.js:27-36, assembled at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/view-model/sort-options.js:8-18). Arrival newest-first is selected when the page loads and there is no unsorted option, so the trader cannot see the list in whatever order the service returns it.

Design release 1's select is labelled "Sort by:" and offers "Select one", "Newest first", "Oldest first" and "Arrival date", in that order and taken from app/data/dashboard-notifications.js:147-152, rendered at app/views/dashboard.html:238-250. "Select one" is what the page loads with, so the design's starting state is an unsorted list and no ordering is named until the trader chooses one. The design names what the trader wants — the newest notifications, the oldest, or the next to arrive — rather than naming a field and a direction.

Replace the four options in src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/copy/copy.en.js:27-36 with the design's three plus an unselected "Select one", and relabel the control "Sort by:". "Newest first" and "Oldest first" map onto the existing createdAt directions and "Arrival date" onto arrivalDate, so src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/dashboard/view-model/sort-options.js:8-18 and the sort parser it feeds change with them. This is copy and the labels behind it, and it lands entirely in Frontend against the design as it already stands, so the band is frontend-work and nothing has to come first. The two runs disagree about that: one folded the option labels into a single sort finding and banded the whole of it disputed, parking the labels behind a designer's answer along with everything else about the control, and the other separated them and banded them frontend-work, which is the band kept here. What turns on it is whether any of the sort work can be done now — relabelling the options is plain copy that lands against the design as it stands, and what is genuinely in dispute is the button and the behaviour, not the labels. What "Select one" means for the list query — that the page can load with no ordering applied at all, which Frontend has no state for — is a behaviour change rather than copy and is raised on its own as inc-031. The three named orderings here can be relabelled without it, and it can be built without them.

increments.title: Design release 1 fills in the country's code as a fixed prefix and asks only for the rest of the region of origin code; Frontend makes the user type the whole code inside five characters.
increments.detail:
Answering Yes reveals one plain text box, five characters wide, labelled "Region of origin code" and hinted "For example, FR-75". The user types the whole code including the country part, and nothing checks that the country part they type matches the country they picked higher up the page. The whole value is capped at five characters (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/controller.js:71-75). For a consignment from France that leaves two characters for the region once "FR-" has been typed, so any region whose code runs longer than two characters cannot be entered at all — IE-DUB, for one, needs six. The field is declared at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/template.njk:24-34.

Answering Yes reveals a field labelled "Enter the region of origin code", hinted "Enter up to 5 characters.", made of two parts: a grey, unfocusable prefix box already showing the two-letter code of the country chosen higher up the page — "FR" in the captured picture — and a text box beside it. The user types only the part after the prefix and has all five characters for it; the service joins the two into the full code. The field is declared at app/views/partials/region-of-origin-code-input.html:14-29 and revealed from app/views/origin-of-the-import.html:102.

On the origin page, derive the prefix from the country the user has already chosen, render it as a govuk-input prefix beside the code box, and collect and validate only the part after it, up to five characters. Relabel the field "Enter the region of origin code" and replace the worked example with "Enter up to 5 characters.". Widening the box on its own is not the fix: the point is that the user cannot get the prefix wrong. Moving the five-character cap from the whole code to the part after the prefix is the substance of the change, and it is what makes longer regional codes enterable. Keep the joined value as what is stored, so nothing downstream has to learn about two fields: Design release 1 upper-cases what the user typed and joins the two parts with a hyphen, so typing "75" with France chosen records "FR-75" (app/routes.js:9239, :9246-9251), while Frontend only trims the box, so build the same normalisation in. How much reference data this needs is the one point the two runs read differently. Frontend already holds the two-letter code as the value of every country option (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/controller.js:57-61), and Design release 1's own prefix map departs from the plain country code only for Ceuta and Melilla, neither of which is in Frontend's list — on that reading nothing new is needed. Against that, Design release 1's prefix table is keyed on its own country label strings, so if the prefix map is lifted across rather than rebuilt from the option values, this change rides on the country list change in inc-081. Settle which of those two routes is being taken before starting.

FALSIFIED BY: A prefix rendered beside Frontend's region of origin code box. The captured DOM of fe-origin-region-code-revealed holds a bare <input class="govuk-input govuk-input--width-5"> with no govuk-input__prefix wrapper and no maxlength; finding either would prove this wrong.

increments.title: DR1 picks the country of origin by typing into a search box that offers matches as you type; the frontend makes the user open a dropdown and scroll a fixed list.
increments.detail:
Country of origin is a govukSelect about a third of the content width. The closed control reads 'Select a country' and opening it gives one long alphabetical list with a divider rule — a disabled row of dashes — under the placeholder. There is no way to type. The user scrolls (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/template.njk:15-22), and the options themselves are assembled in the origin controller (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/controller.js:57-61).

DR1 renders a full-width search input with the placeholder 'Search for a country' and a magnifying-glass button. Typing filters a results list that appears under the box, and choosing a result writes the country into a hidden field and leaves its name sitting visibly in the box — the captured revealed state shows 'France' in the search box; a live region announces the match count to screen readers. The list it searches carries regions as well as states, so 'Spain' surfaces Spain, Canary Islands, Ceuta and Melilla together (app/views/origin-of-the-import.html:53-98).

Replace the select with the same search-and-choose control DR1 uses: a full-width search input labelled as now, a results list that filters as the user types, and the chosen country left visible in the box. Keep a no-JavaScript fallback: DR1's control degrades to a bare text input, which the real service cannot ship, so the fallback has to be a select or a server-rendered results page. The frontend also has to grow the underlying list to match DR1, and it is worth doing that first — a search box over 31 entries buys less than a search box over the 41 DR1 offers — though that sequencing is not agreed. The second run read the differing country lists as fixture data on both sides and scoped its version of this finding to the control alone, on the reasoning that both sides simply read a list and what is at stake here is how the user reaches an entry in it; the lists themselves are argued separately in inc-081. Either way, the country the user picks has to be readable by the region-of-origin code field, because DR1 derives that field's prefix from the chosen country (inc-079), so build the picker so that choosing a country can drive the prefix. Nothing has to land before the control change itself: the country list is already in the frontend's countries service.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding that DR1's country of origin renders as a plain select for a DR1 session, with the search module mounted only under a design-release-2 flag.

increments.title: Frontend lets a user answer Yes to the region of origin question and continue with the code box left empty; Design release 1 holds them on the page until they enter it.
increments.detail:
The revealed code box is checked for length and nothing else. The origin page's rule set requires a country, accepts either answer to the region question, and applies a maximum-length rule to the code and two rules to the internal reference — there is no presence rule for the code at all (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/controller.js:63-82). So a user can select Yes, leave the box empty, press Save and continue, and reach the next page having recorded no region of origin code, with no message anywhere on the way. The page is perfectly able to show an error — fe-origin-error is the same page holding a user back for a missing country — so this is a missing rule rather than a missing mechanism.

Submitting the origin page with Yes selected and the code box empty re-renders the page with "There is a problem" at the top and "Enter the region of origin code" both in the error summary and against the code field, the summary link moving focus into the box (app/routes.js:254-260). Answering No skips the question and nothing is asked. It is the only rule Design release 1 states for this page, but Design release 1 also carries the same requirement at the two later points Frontend uses: the hub reads the origin task as complete only when the code is present under Yes (app/routes.js:231-245), and Continue on the review page is refused while it is missing (app/routes.js:10068-10075). Design release 1 therefore enforces at all three points and Frontend only at the last two.

Add a presence rule to the region of origin code that fires only when the region question is answered Yes, with the message "Enter the region of origin code" in the summary and against the field, and add that message to the origin feature's copy alongside the length message already there (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/copy/copy.en.js:21-26). The point is that the message arrives when the user makes the mistake rather than as a stuck hub row later. Leave the No branch alone. Nothing has to land first. Design release 1's origin page was not photographed in its error state, so the observation that would settle the wording and the anchor is that page submitted with Yes chosen and the code box empty. The obligation behind the field is already right and must not be touched: it is marked mandatory whenever the requirement is Yes (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/obligations/sections/origin.js:27-36), which is why the notification cannot be submitted with the box empty. This is a validator change on one page, not a model change — nothing downstream moves and nothing needs a new pattern. All that is missing is the page-level rule that tells the user so at the point of the mistake.

FALSIFIED BY: Submitting fe-origin with Yes selected and the code box empty and being held on the page with an error. Frontend's origin validator composes exactly one required rule (for the country), one either-or rule for the radio and two maximum-length rules, so the code's presence is never checked; a page that refused that submission would prove this wrong.

C is more honest about its evidence — it records that DR1's origin page was never photographed in its error state and names the observation that would settle the wording. increments.title: DR1 shows the draft status and the notification reference from the first page of a new notification; the frontend withholds both until the first answer is saved.
increments.detail:
A strip carrying a blue "Draft" tag and the notification reference sits above the page heading on 29 of the 33 captured screens. Origin of the import is the one journey page without it: on a brand-new notification the page shows the heading with nothing above it, so the user starting a notification cannot see its reference until they have saved the first page. The strip is suppressed deliberately — src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/controller.js:88-89 passes the journey to the layout through `journeyIfStarted`, which only yields it once the notification has committed answers on the test at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/flow/entry-guard.js:37, and src/server/app/shared/layout.njk:65-70 renders nothing when it is absent.

DR1's origin page shows the strip unconditionally: a "Draft" tag and the reference GBN-AG-26-7K8M2P sit between the back link and the caption, exactly as they do on every later page. The view includes the shared status partial with no guard at all — app/views/origin-of-the-import.html:29 — and app/views/partials/notification-status.html:18-24 defaults the status text to "Draft" when nothing has set one, which is what makes the strip work on a notification that has not been touched yet. DR1 does not carry the strip on every screen: it is absent from the dashboard, the address-book pages, the declaration, the submitted page and the transporter-add pages, all of which sit outside a notification in progress.

Render the status strip on Origin of the import from the first request, by dropping the committed-answers guard at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/controller.js:88-89 so the journey always reaches the layout — pass it to kit.base at :107 directly rather than through `journeyIfStarted`. Nothing else has to change: the tag and the reference the strip prints already come from src/server/app/shared/kit.js:53-58, which needs only the journey. Nothing blocks it either: the reference already exists when the page is first drawn. Starting a notification posts to the backend, which mints the reference and returns the created record, and the user is only then redirected to the origin page under that reference — so the reference is in the page's own URL before a single answer is saved. The guard is a presentation choice, not a symptom of a missing reference. The back-link target on the same page is computed from the same condition and is correct as it stands — a fresh notification's back link goes to the dashboard — so change only the strip, keeping `backLinkFor` on the committed-answers test.

FALSIFIED BY: Loading Origin of the import on a notification with no saved answers and seeing a Draft tag and reference above the heading.

increments.title: Frontend sets the origin page's three question labels smaller than Design release 1 does, and renders the internal-reference one at body weight so it does not read as a question.
increments.detail:
The origin page asks three questions and gives them three different weights. "Country of origin" and "Does the consignment have a region of origin code?" are set at the small label size, and "Your internal reference for this consignment (optional)" carries no size at all, so it renders in ordinary body text the same size as the hint below it and reads as a sentence rather than a question — on the page shot that question and its hint read as a single paragraph, told apart only by colour. All three are set in src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/origin/template.njk:18, :38 and :46-51.

All three questions are set at the medium heading size and in bold, so the page reads as three questions with their hints and controls beneath them — three sections under one h1 that the eye finds without reading: "Country of origin" as a heading at app/views/origin-of-the-import.html:46, the region-of-origin legend at :126 and the internal-reference label at :155.

Raise all three question labels on the origin page to the medium size: the country control's label, the region-of-origin fieldset legend, and the internal reference input's label. One template, three classes. If a service-wide heading scale is being settled elsewhere, take that instead — the point is that the page's questions are all one size, not that they are this particular size. Nothing has to land first, and it is independent of the country picker and region code changes on the same page — do it in the same pass if those are being made.

increments.title: What a user is offered at the foot of a journey page follows no single rule on either side: the frontend gives some pages three controls and others one, and Design release 1 gives its own sibling pages three, two or one
increments.detail:
A trader filling in a notification meets one of six different endings to a page, and cannot predict which. On 41 of the 67 captured frontend screens the page ends with three controls — a primary button, a secondary "Save and return to hub" button and a "Cancel and return to hub" link. On the other 26 the page offers no way to save what has been entered and leave. The two return controls always travel together: on every screen where either appears the other does too, because one shared macro builds all three unconditionally and takes no argument that would drop one (src/server/app/shared/save-actions.njk:3-13).

What decides which pages get them is not anything a user can see. Nineteen feature templates call that macro, and they are exactly the nineteen answer pages of the linear flow other than the dashboard (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/flow/flow.js:31-86). Anything routed outside that flow ends the page its own way. So the split falls inside a single section of the service: the CPH number page and the five party pickers are both reached from rows on the consignment addresses page, and the CPH page offers all three controls while Place of origin offers only "Save and continue" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/_address-picker.njk:109, its label duplicated in a copy key of its own at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/copy/copy.en.js:62). A trader who wants to stop halfway can do it on one and not on the other.

The primary beside them is not one button either but three labels out of four copy keys: "Save and continue" from the shared key on 30 screens (src/server/app/shared/copy.en.js:42-45), "Save and finish" on the four animal-identification states (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/animal-identification/animal-identification.njk:25), and "Continue" on the seven documents and consignment-addresses states (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/documents/template.njk:92 and src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/template.njk:16).

The 26 screens with no return control break down as nine party-picker states ending with a lone "Save and continue"; five check-your-answers and declaration states ending with a lone "Continue" (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/check-answers/template.njk:112 and src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/declaration/template.njk:42); the delete-notification and cancel-amendment confirmations, which pair a primary with a secondary link back; and ten overview, dashboard and confirmation states, which carry page-specific controls rather than the journey pattern and sit outside this finding. Giving a party picker the return controls is not a template edit alone: its post always redirects to the consignment addresses page and never reads the exit value the secondary button submits (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/party-picker.controller.js:92, against the shared helpers at src/server/app/shared/kit.js:77-89).

Design release 1 offers no rule to copy, because it does not follow one itself. Across its 60 captured screens the three-control ending appears on 29; the primary reads "Save and continue" on 45 screens and "Continue" on 7; and the cancel control has three destinations rather than one — "Cancel and return to overview" as a link on the 29, "Cancel and return to dashboard" as a secondary button on three, and "Cancel and return to address book" as a secondary button on three. Unlike the frontend, the two return controls do not travel together here: six screens offer a way to cancel and no way to save and return.

The inconsistency lands inside the design's own structures, so no reading of it produces a rule. Of the twelve pages the overview links to (app/routes.js:5749-5841), ten end with all three controls, but origin-of-the-import ends with a single "Save and continue" — inside the very same form-actions wrapper the three-control pages use, with the second button and the cancel paragraph simply absent (app/views/origin-of-the-import.html:167-175) — and contact-address-for-consignment ends with a bare "Continue" (app/views/contact-address-for-consignment.html:86). Below the consignment-parties row its three sibling sub-pages disagree with each other: permanent-address-animals carries all three (app/views/permanent-address-animals.html:104-120), cph-number carries one "Save and continue" (app/views/cph-number.html:55-58) and consignment-address-select carries one (app/views/consignment-address-select.html:167-170). In transport the type chooser ends with a bare "Continue" (app/views/transporter-add.html:86) while the two forms below it end with "Save and continue" beside a secondary "Cancel and return to dashboard" (app/views/transporter-add-private.html:46-51), a destination that appears nowhere else in the notification journey.

There is no shared partial behind any of this. Eleven root views hand-write the block, nine of them repeating the same wrapper classes verbatim and two writing their own — app/views/consignment-details.html:136-154 against app/views/permanent-address-animals.html:104-120 — and the only journey-form-actions partials in the codebase belong to later releases, which no root view includes, so DR1 never had one place to state the rule in.

The design's own routing says the single-button pages are omissions rather than decisions. Fifteen post handlers accept the hub action that the secondary button submits, covering nineteen of the design's post routes (app/routes.js:1315-1317), and the handler behind origin-of-the-import is one of them: send it that action and it saves and redirects to the overview (app/routes.js:9265-9268). The page renders no button that would send it.

One arrangement difference runs through all 29: Design release 1 puts the two buttons on a row and the cancel link in a paragraph beneath them, where the frontend puts all three on one line.

Make the ending of a journey page the same everywhere, on one rule, and apply it from one place. This replaces the earlier reading of the same evidence, which proposed stripping the return controls from the five frontend pages Design release 1 happens to end with one button; that would have copied the design's own inconsistency into the frontend rather than removing it, and it was dropped for that reason. Nothing here changes what any control says.

Deciding the rule needs a service owner, and that is why this is banded disputed: Design release 1 is signed off but does not state one, and neither of the two candidate rules can be read off it. The two are:

(a) Every page that collects an answer ends with the same three controls. Under this the frontend is nineteen-twentieths of the way there and the work is to bring the five party pickers into line: call the shared macro from src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/_address-picker.njk:109 instead of a bare button, and route the exit value through kit.exitTarget in src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/party-picker/party-picker.controller.js:92 so the secondary button has somewhere to go. The per-picker copy key at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/addresses/copy/copy.en.js:62 becomes dead and goes.

(b) Only the pages the overview links to end with the three controls, and a page reached from another page ends with the primary alone. Under this the party pickers stay as they are and seven pages lose their return controls — the second-and-later pages of the task rows at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/flow/task-rows.js:27-59, namely consignment details, import purpose, port of exit, exit date, transporter selection, private transporter details and CPH number.

The mechanism is the same either way and belongs in the shared macro, not in copies of a shortened button group. Give src/server/app/shared/save-actions.njk:3-13 a fourth parameter, showReturnControls, defaulting to true, and wrap the secondary button and the cancel link in it. Under (a) no template passes it and the party pickers adopt the macro; under (b) the seven templates named above pass false — src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/cph-number/template.njk:25, src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/consignment-details/consignment-details.njk:31, src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/import-purpose/template.njk:24, src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/port-of-exit/template.njk:23, src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/exit-date/template.njk:15, src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/transport/transporters-select/transporters-select.njk:25 and src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/transport/private-transporter-details/private-transporter-details.njk:92 — and the party pickers adopt the macro passing false, so that every ending in the service comes out of one file. Whichever rule is chosen, the review section and the two confirmation pages keep the endings they have: check your answers and the declaration read "Continue" alone on both sides already, and delete and cancel-amendment are confirm-or-go-back pages that Design release 1 does not have.

What would settle the choice is a ruling on one sentence: may a trader stop and save from every page that asks a question, or only from the pages the overview sends them to. Design release 1 answers it both ways on adjacent pages of the same section, so the answer has to come from the service owner rather than from the design.

Two boundaries with neighbouring findings, both of which change what these controls say and neither of which changes where they appear. service-wide--primary-button-says-continue-not-save-and-continue owns the text of the primary button. service-wide--save-and-cancel-buttons-name-the-hub owns the text of the two return controls. This finding changes no string at all; it changes which pages render the controls, and it is the only one of the three that needs a decision before it can start. Order does not matter between them: the renames touch copy keys and this touches the macro's parameters and its callers. One knock-on worth flagging to whoever picks up the renames: if rule (b) is chosen, the two return controls end up on seven fewer pages than they are on today — twelve fewer captured screens, because four of those seven pages were photographed in more than one state — so the rename lands on 29 frontend screens rather than 41.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding a shared partial or macro in Design release 1's root views that renders the end-of-page controls — one file every root journey view includes — which would mean the design does state a single rule and the work is to follow it rather than to choose one.

finding.verification:
Verified by a different agent than wrote it, against the two pinned checkouts (git rev-parse confirms the frontend at 76a864ba93ac7c60d358c902bd68396731daacf3 and the prototype at 491b39263e4f3b613bc398851b701425b74438ee) and against all 67 frontend and 60 Design release 1 files under capture/html/. The central claim survives. Six numbers or sentences were wrong and are corrected in the slots; each is named below.

Counts re-derived here rather than taken from the author. "Save and return to hub" and "Cancel and return to hub" each match 41 of the 67 frontend captures, and sorting the two file lists and diffing them returns nothing, so the two controls never appear apart — that is the whole of the travel-together claim, checked rather than asserted. The 26 remainder, listed with grep -L, are the nine party-picker states, three check-answers states, two declaration states, fe-delete-notification, fe-cancel-amend, seven dashboard states, two hub states and fe-confirmation: the author's 9 / 5 / 2 / 10 breakdown exactly. On the requirements side "Save and return to overview" and "Cancel and return to overview" each match 29 of the 60 captures and the same files; "Cancel and return to dashboard" matches three and "Cancel and return to address book" three, and diffing every file carrying "Save and return to" against every file carrying "Cancel and return to" leaves exactly those six, so three destinations and six cancel-without-save both hold. Primary labels on that side: 45 files carry "Save and continue" and seven carry a bare "Continue" (declaration and its error state, review-notification and its incomplete state, transporter-add, contact-address-for-consignment, address-book-add).

The strongest claim — the 19-to-19 correspondence — is exact. Grepping src/server for saveActions returns 19 invocation sites in 19 feature templates. Listing the pages of src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/flow/flow.js:31-86 by hand gives 23: dashboardPage, the three review pages (notificationViewPage, declarationPage, confirmationPage) and 19 others. I matched those 19 one-for-one onto the 19 templates with nothing left over on either side. The party-picker template is the twentieth answer-collecting template and it is the one that does not call the macro, which is what "nineteen-twentieths" means and it is fair.

The decisive claim survives at source, and I attacked it three ways. app/routes.js:1315-1317 is isJourneySoftSaveAction, true for 'hub' and for 'review'. Grep returns 16 call sites besides the definition; reading the enclosing handler for each gives 15 post handlers, because reason-for-import tests it twice (:10216 and :10268), and one of the 15 is handleConsignmentAddressSelectPost at :3838, registered on all five selectable consignment-address sections at :10914-10919, so 19 post routes accept it. The author wrote "sixteen post handlers"; the slot now reads fifteen handlers over nineteen routes. The origin half is sound: router.post('/origin-of-the-import') writes countryOfOrigin, regionOfOriginRequired and internalReference into the session at :9242-9244 before reaching :9265-9268, so action=hub does save and then redirect to /notification-hub, skipping validation to do it. app/views/origin-of-the-import.html renders exactly one govukButton, at :169-173, inside the same app-origin-form-actions wrapper the three-control pages use; grepping that whole file for 'action' returns only the macro import, the form's own action attribute and that one button. Nothing on the page can send it.

The partial claim, which the whole finding rests on, holds. find over app/ for *form-actions* returns only app/views/partials/design-release-2/journey-form-actions.html and app/views/partials/design-release-2.1/journey-form-actions.html; grepping every view outside those two release subfolders for journey-form-actions returns nothing at all, so no root view includes either; and neither app/views/layouts/main.html nor app/views/layouts/journey.html contains a govukButton, a form-actions wrapper or a cancel link. app/views/ holds exactly 30 root .html files and exactly 11 contain "Save and return to overview", so 11 of 30 is right. But "each with its own wrapper markup" was wrong: nine of the eleven repeat app-origin-form-actions, app-origin-actions and app-origin-form-actions__cancel verbatim, and only permanent-address-animals and transporter write their own names — the pair the author chose as the example happens to be one of the two that differ. Corrected; it does not weaken the finding, because eleven hand-written copies remain eleven places to edit.

Read app/routes.js:5749-5841 line by line: twelve overview items across six sections, counting both conditional ones. Intersected against the eleven three-control views: ten match, and the two that do not are origin-of-the-import and contact-address-for-consignment, as claimed. permanent-address-animals is the eleventh three-control view and the overview does not link to it, which the finding implies and does not overstate. The three consignment-parties siblings check out at source — app/views/permanent-address-animals.html:104-122 all three, app/views/cph-number.html:55-58 one, app/views/consignment-address-select.html:166-169 one — with one qualification left in the record rather than in the prose: a secondary "Add a new address" govukButton sits immediately above that last primary at :160-164, so "carries one" there means one control in the save-and-return sense, not one button on the page.

Both corrections to the dropped inc-106 hold. dr1-transporter-add-private.html:581 and dr1-transporter-add-commercial.html:490 each render "Cancel and return to dashboard" as a submit button carrying name=action and value=cancel with govuk-button--secondary — a button, not the link inc-106 called it — and inc-106's prose names only the private page, so it did miss the commercial one. Source agrees at app/views/transporter-add-private.html:44-56.

The "four primaries" claim was wrong and is corrected to three. Within the 41 the labels are "Save and continue" on 30 (39 frontend files carry the string, nine of them party pickers outside the 41), "Save and finish" on the four animal-identification states, and "Continue" on the four documents and three addresses-hub states: 30 + 4 + 7 = 41. increments.title: Frontend asks what is being imported by printing the whole commodity reference list as tick boxes; Design release 1 asks the user to search for a commodity and shows nothing until they do.
increments.detail:
The page has no search box. Under the heading "What are you importing?" it prints every commodity the reference service knows about, one tick-box group per commodity, legend "Cow (0102)", "Horse (0101)", "Cat (01061900)", "Dog (01061900)", "Fish (0301)", with a tick box per species inside each. The template loops the whole list and renders a govukCheckboxes group for each entry with no filtering step of any kind (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/search/search.njk:19-30), and the view model builds one group per commodity with no query argument (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/search/view-model/commodity-groups.js:3-15). The controller takes no query parameter and has no search action: it renders the list on GET and validates the ticked boxes on POST (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/search/search.controller.js:36-52). Nothing narrows the list, nothing summarises what has been picked, and the only way to review a selection is to scroll the fieldsets looking for ticks. The captured page fits on one screen only because the stub holds five commodities and eight species between them.

The page shows one control, a search box labelled "Search for a commodity" with the hint "You can search by common name (for example, cattle), commodity code (0102), or Latin name (Bos taurus)." The label is set at heading size — it is the input's own label carrying the design's heading class rather than a heading in its own right — and the box carries a magnifying-glass button. Nothing is listed until the user has typed at least three characters: results then appear in a panel directly under the box, grouped under a commodity header such as "Cattle (0102)" with a tick box per matching species, and the matched characters are shown in bold. Chosen species collect into a panel below the results, headed with a running count — "2 selected" — that lists each one and offers "Clear all", so the user always sees what is on the notification without scrolling a list. The search matches on the species Latin name, the species common name, the commodity name and the commodity code (app/views/what-are-you-importing.html:47-117). Selections survive leaving and re-entering the page, because they are seeded back into the control as JSON (app/views/what-are-you-importing.html:110-114).

Replace the printed tick-box list on the commodity page with a search: a labelled search box over the reference list, a results panel that appears once at least three characters are entered and groups matching species under their commodity heading with a tick box each, and a running list of what has been chosen so far, headed with the count, with a way to clear it. The list the frontend prints today is bounded only by what the reference service returns — the requirements side's own fixture already carries twenty-one commodities and over a hundred species under "Other live mammals" alone — so the printed list stops being usable as soon as the stub is replaced. Nothing has to land first: the reference data the search would filter is the same list the page already fetches. Keep the existing "Select a commodity" error, which both sides already use for an empty submission. Run A sequences the same work differently: a search box over eight species is a search box over nothing, so on its reading the control is worth little until the real catalogue is sourced, and species want their common names first if searching by common name is to return anything.

FALSIFIED BY: A search input, a filter field or a type-ahead anywhere on fe-commodity-search. The captured DOM for that page contains no input other than the CSRF hidden field and the eight species tick boxes, and the controller reads no query parameter, so finding one would prove this wrong.

increments.title: Frontend's "Help with commodity codes" gives one sentence and no way to look a code up; Design release 1 explains what a commodity code is and links out to the Trade Tariff tool.
increments.detail:
Opening the "Help with commodity codes" details reveals a single sentence — "Commodity codes are used to classify goods for import and export." — and nothing else. It is passed to the govukDetails macro as plain text, so it cannot carry a link (src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/search/search.njk:31-34, with the string at src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/features/commodities/copy/copy.en.js:9). A user who does not know their commodity code is told what one is and left with no way to find it.

The details of the same name, in the same position on the page, holds three paragraphs: "Commodity codes are internationally recognised reference numbers.", "A commodity code describes a specific product when importing or exporting goods.", and "You can look up commodity codes using the Trade Tariff tool (opens in a new tab).", where "Trade Tariff tool" is a link to https://www.gov.uk/trade-tariff opening in a new tab (app/views/what-are-you-importing.html:119-132).

Replace the one-sentence help text with Design release 1's three paragraphs, including the Trade Tariff link and its "(opens in a new tab)" suffix. That means passing HTML to the details rather than text, so the copy entry changes shape as well as wording; the Welsh copy file beside it carries the same single string and needs the same treatment. Nothing has to land first — the link is a public GOV.UK page.

FALSIFIED BY: A link out to the Trade Tariff tool, or any other commodity-code lookup, reachable from the frontend's commodity page. The captured DOM for fe-commodity-search contains exactly one link inside the main content — "Cancel and return to hub" — and no commodity-code lookup anywhere in the frontend's source.
